profile.name: Geommu
profile.tagline: Korean court sword dance of twin blades, metallic ringings, and swirling silk sleeves.
profile.insight: Danced by female performers wielding paired metallic short swords equipped with ringing brass rings, Geommu was preserved as South Korea's 12th Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1967.
profile.profile: Geommu is a traditional Korean sword dance originating in the Three Kingdoms period and later refined into a formal royal court tradition during the Joseon Dynasty. Executed by six to eight female dancers clad in stylized military hanbok and red-tasselled headgear, the dance features dual short swords with metal rings that sound with every motion. Performers manipulate extended striped silk sleeves before picking up the unsharpened blades to execute floor patterns, kneeling stances, and circular rotations. Accompanied by the wind-and-percussion ensemble Samhyeon-nyukgak, Geommu balances sharp martial symbolism with fluid, elegant motion.
profile.profile_long:
Geommu trace its origins to the Three Kingdoms era around 660 AD, anchored in dual legends recorded in historical chronicles such as the Samguk yusa and Donggyeong japgi. In Silla lore, a young sword dancer named Hwangchang performed before the king of Baekje and assassinated him in an act of defiance, leading to his execution; the people of Silla honored his memory by performing sword dances wearing masks resembling his face, giving birth to Hwangchangmu. A parallel Silla legend attributes the dance to Gwanchang, a sixteen-year-old archer-warrior whose death in battle against Baekje inspired memorial sword dances. Over centuries, the tradition evolved from a masked martial folk form into an elite performance art.

During the Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910), Geommu underwent a transformation when the Royal Court rearranged the dance and transferred its practice to the Kisaeng—female court entertainers. Trained through formalized institutions known as Gwonbeon, the Kisaeng discarded the traditional face masks and adapted the dance into an elegant, primarily female court ritual. To eliminate the risk of accidental injury during delicate choreographies, rigid metal blades were replaced with replica short swords known as ssang dan geom, kal, or dangeom. During the Japanese occupation of Korea (1910–1945), transmission of the tradition ceased. In the 1950s, cultural promoter Park Heonbong led eight veteran female dancers to reconstruct Jinju Geommu, leading to its designation in 1967 as South Korea's 12th Important Intangible Cultural Property.

Geommu relies on two structural foundations: chum-sawi (dance motions) and changdan (rhythmic cycles). A typical performance moves through three primary positional motifs: Ipchum-sawi, where six to eight dancers form two facing parallel lines; Anjeon-sawi, where the dancers drop to their knees while maintaining their facing lines; and Yeonpungdae, where performers form a circle and rotate smoothly in coordinated patterns. Before picking up their weapons, dancers utilize saektonghansam—extended striped sleeve covers tied at the wrists—to throw, wave, and drop graceful arcs of silk. Western observer Horace Newton Allen noted in 1896 that dancers executed spins around swords placed on the floor before picking them up as the music accelerated, whirling the blades rapidly to create an illusion of piercing movement.

The dance is accompanied by Samhyeon-nyukgak, a six-instrument ensemble consisting of two piri (double-reed bamboo oboes), one daegeum (large transverse bamboo flute), one haegeum (two-stringed fiddle), one janggu (hourglass drum), and one buk (barrel drum). The music follows dynamic changdan rhythmic cycles anchored by the contrasting deep and crisp tones of the janggu's leather heads and the wooden stick strikes on the buk. As the wind instruments play melancholic yet driving melodies, the rhythm gradually accelerates, driving the visual energy of the spinning dancers.

The attire worn in Geommu is a stylized version of Joseon Dynasty military uniforms. Dancers wear a full hanbok composed of a chima (skirt) and jeogori (jacket), overlaid with a military coat called a kwaeja or jeonbok, secured across the chest with a wide red sash known as a jeon-dae or hongtti. On their heads rests a jeon-rip (military cap) adorned with a red tassel and dangling strings of red and yellow beads bound beneath the chin over thick white traditional socks called beoseon. Regional variations feature distinct color schemes: Jinju Geommu traditionally uses a blue or dark blue chima with a jade green or light jeogori, whereas Gwangju in Jeolla Province displays a vibrant red chima paired with a light green jeogori. The weapons, made of baektong (a nickel and white brass alloy), measure 22 centimeters in length and feature three loose rings between blade and hilt that clink musically throughout the dance.

Today, Geommu is preserved and taught at institutions such as the Jinju Muhyeong Munhwajae Jeonsu Hoegwan, private academies in Jinju, and the National Gugak Center in Seoul. Beyond formal stage revivals, Jinju Geommu plays a central role in annual commemorative rituals honoring Nongae, a historic kisaeng who sacrificed her life during the Japanese invasions by casting herself off a cliff alongside an enemy general.

sections.origins_and_history: Legend traces Geommu to the Three Kingdoms period around 660 AD in Silla. Chronicled in sources like Samguk yusa and Donggyeong japgi, tales tell of Hwangchang (a boy sword dancer who killed the king of Baekje and was executed) and Gwanchang (a young Hwarang warrior slain in battle). Memorial dances wearing masks imitating Hwangchang were known as Hwangchangmu. During the Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910), the Royal Court reorganized the dance and assigned it to Kisaeng court entertainers trained in Gwonbeon academies. The Kisaeng dropped the masks, adapted the performance for female dancers, and introduced replica short swords. After transmission halted under Japanese rule (1910–1945), Park Heonbong gathered eight female dancers in the 1950s to reconstruct Jinju Geommu, securing its status in 1967 as South Korea's 12th Important Intangible Cultural Property.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Geommu is performed by a group of 6 to 8 female dancers working through chum-sawi (dance movements) and changdan (rhythmic cycles). Performance centers on three primary movement patterns: Ipchum-sawi (dancers standing in two facing rows), Anjeon-sawi (dancers executing floorwork while kneeling in the two-row formation), and Yeonpungdae (dancers forming a circular pattern and spinning in rotation). Dancers initially manipulate long striped sleeve extensions (saektonghansam) while swords rest on the floor, later lifting the twin short swords (ssang dan geom) to execute rapid, controlled spins and spatial figures as the musical tempo accelerates.
sections.music_and_instruments: Geommu is accompanied by Samhyeon-nyukgak, a traditional six-instrument ensemble comprising two piri (bamboo double-reed oboes), one daegeum (large bamboo transverse flute), one haegeum (two-string bowed fiddle), one janggu (double-headed hourglass drum), and one buk (barrel drum). The janggu uses different leather skins on each head to produce distinct pitches, while the buk is struck with an open hand and a wooden stick. The ensemble provides changing changdan rhythmic cycles characterized by specific meters, speeds, and structural accents.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear a stylized Joseon Dynasty military uniform over a hanbok. The costume consists of a chima (skirt), jeogori (jacket), kwaeja or jeonbok (military overcoat), and jeon-dae or hongtti (wide red chest sash). Dancers wear a black military-style cap (jeon-rip or jeollip) tied under the chin with dangling red and yellow beads and a red tassel, along with thick white socks (beoseon) and detachable striped sleeve covers (saektonghansam). Regional variants dictate skirt and jacket colors, such as Jinju's blue skirt and jade green jacket. Dancers carry paired short swords (dangeom/kal) made of nickel-brass alloy (baektong) measuring 22 cm, featuring three attached rings between hilt and blade that sound during movement.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a memorial and court entertainment performance, Geommu bridges military symbolism and theatrical elegance. In Jinju, the dance is prominently performed during an annual memorial ritual honoring Nongae, a patriot kisaeng who died taking a Japanese general off a cliff during wartime. Modern performances take place at cultural heritage centers, national theaters, and traditional arts festivals.
sections.notable_figures: Historical accounts credit Horace Newton Allen with writing the first detailed Western eyewitness description of the dance in 1896. In the 1950s, traditional cultural promoter Park Heonbong led the reconstruction of Jinju Geommu by interviewing and working with eight surviving female dancers.
sections.regional_variants: Jinju Geommu is the primary court-derived variant, originating in Jinju and characterized by blue skirts and jade green jackets. Gwangju in Jeolla Province presents a regional costume variant featuring a red skirt and light green jacket.
sections.lineage: Traces from ancient Silla sword rituals and Hwangchangmu mask dances to Joseon court Kisaeng repertoire taught at Gwonbeon institutions, preserved today as Intangible Cultural Property No. 12.

basic_steps: Ipchum-sawi: Form two parallel rows facing your partner, standing tall with arms extended in saektonghansam sleeves.
Sleeve release and floor passage: Perform controlled sleeve waves around swords lying on the floor.
Anjeon-sawi: Lower smoothly onto knees maintaining the two facing rows, keeping upper body upright.
Sword lift: Lift the twin short swords (ssang dan geom) from the floor while maintaining knee placement or standing up.
Yeonpungdae: Form a large group circle and rotate smoothly in spatial coordination while twirling the short blades.
teaching.rhythm: Accompanied by Changdan rhythmic cycles led by Janggu and Buk drums, accelerating progressively from slow meter to rapid tempo.
teaching.formation: Group dance of 6 to 8 performers starting in two facing parallel rows and transitioning into circular formations.
teaching.level_notes: Requires strong quad control for kneeling drops (Anjeon-sawi), upper body coordination for sleeve extensions, and precise wrist dexterity for short-sword twirling.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Changdan cycles defined by dual-pitched Janggu strokes and accentuating Buk strikes.
music_profile.musical_form: Samhyeon-nyukgak suite structure transitioning through distinct changdan rhythmic phases.
music_profile.sound_description: A wind-and-percussion soundscape dominated by the resonant bamboo reeding of twin piri and the breathy transverse tones of the daegeum, underpinned by the dual-pitched skin tones of the janggu drum, punctuated by the metallic clinking of sword rings.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, graceful court posture with broad shoulder carriage to accommodate military overcoats and headpiece balance.
movement_profile.footwork: Smooth gliding step executed in thick white socks (beoseon) without outer shoes, progressing into swift circular walking and floor pivots.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Fluid arm swoops using extended striped sleeve covers (saektonghansam), shifting to rapid hilt twirling of twin short blades.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Controlled torso stability during kneeling drops; slight fluid rotation of upper body during sword flourishes.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Transitions between two facing parallel lines (Ipchum-sawi, Anjeon-sawi) and a revolving group circle (Yeonpungdae).
movement_profile.partnering: Non-contact spatial alignment facing a partner across two parallel lines.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Starts stately and expansive, gradually shifting to rapid, exhilarating twirling as drum tempos build.

signature_moves.name: Ipchum-sawi
signature_moves.description: Standing dance motion performed in two parallel lines facing one another.

signature_moves.name: Anjeon-sawi
signature_moves.description: Kneeling dance motion executed while preserving the two facing rows.

signature_moves.name: Yeonpungdae
signature_moves.description: Circular formation movement where dancers rotate and turn in unison.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Level shifts between upright standing postures and low kneeling floorwork (Anjeon-sawi); no high jumps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid sudden uncoordinated wrist snaps that cause erratic sword ring clattering; maintain smooth torso balance while dropping into kneeling positions.

social_formats.description: Group performance by 6 to 8 dancers in facing rows and circular paths.

episode_brief.title_hook: Blades of the Royal Court: The Legacy of Geommu
episode_brief.logline: Explore how ancient Silla sword legends transformed into one of South Korea's most treasured court dance traditions.
beats: Opening visual of metallic short-sword rings clinking against baektong blades in Jinju.
Historical breakdown of Silla warrior legends (Hwangchang and Gwanchang) and Joseon Kisaeng court institutions.
Demonstration of the Samhyeon-nyukgak six-instrument ensemble and Changdan drum patterns.
Step-by-step breakdown of sleeve manipulation (saektonghansam) and floor sword pickup.
Transition from facing row formations (Ipchum-sawi) into circular rotations (Yeonpungdae).
Full group performance of Jinju Geommu in traditional military hanbok attire.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master facing line alignment and sleeve movements.
drills: Practice standing posture with extended arms while wearing sleeve extensions.
Execute basic forward gliding steps in beoseon socks.
Learn Ipchum-sawi facing line spatial positioning.

lesson_ladder.goal: Integrate kneeling transitions and replica sword handling.
drills: Practice Anjeon-sawi knee drops with vertical torso alignment.
Practice smooth floor pickups of twin short swords.
Twirl short swords to generate consistent metallic ring sounds.

lesson_ladder.goal: Perform full group circular rotations (Yeonpungdae) at accelerated tempo.
drills: Practice synchronized circular rotation in group formation.
Combine swift foot pivots with continuous blade twirling.
Execute full performance piece following Changdan acceleration.

visual_motifs: Red-tasselled military caps and bead chin straps.
Ringing nickel-brass sword rings in close-up motion.
Juxtaposition of blue and red hanbok skirts against wooden courtyard floors.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An authoritative master dancer from a Korean intangible cultural heritage preservation center, blending historical precision with graceful demonstration.
episode_brief.music_cue: Opens with solo piri melody over janggu changdan beats, accelerating into full Samhyeon-nyukgak ensemble accompaniment.

seniors.seated_version: Perform Ipchum-sawi upper-body arm swoops and wrist blade twirling while seated firmly in a chair.
seniors.standing_version: Perform facing line arm movements and sword flourishes while maintaining a steady standing base without deep knee drops.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Maintain a moderate, steady tempo; limit arm extensions to shoulder height.
avoid: Deep kneeling drops (Anjeon-sawi) and rapid circular spinning movements.

children.game_version: Sleeve and Ring Tag: Children practice waving sleeve extensions and sounding toy sword rings in coordinated row patterns.
avoid: Sharp metallic props and long static kneeling postures.
